series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.5 · November 2026
title: Carbon Prices Cut Emissions

slides.title: Carbon Prices Cut Emissions
slides.subtitle: What ten natural experiments show about fuel taxes, carbon prices and subsidy reform
slides.message: Every well-measured case shows a cut. In transport and heating, about 1–2% less use per $10 a tonne, building up over five to fifteen years; in power, where gas could replace coal, five to ten times more per dollar. Design matters as much as the price.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.title: Models set carbon-tax plans; these ten cases show what real price rises did

stats.label: natural experiments, 1991–2022: carbon taxes, fuel taxes, emissions trading, a subsidy reform and a price shock
carbon price, or the dollar-per-tonne equivalent of the price rise, per tonne of CO₂

slides.text: Each case has a credible counterfactual: similar countries, provinces or plants without the policy, or tax changes timed independently of the trend. For each: the fuels covered, the rise in retail prices, its carbon price and the measured cut.

slides.title: In transport and heating, every case shows a cut that builds over years

slides.title: In power and industry the cuts were larger for the price; short shocks bought less
slides.note: Eleven further episodes, among them Australia 2012–14, Finland 1990 and France 2014–18, point the same way on thinner evidence.
slides.source: Dechezleprêtre et al. (2023); Colmer et al. (2025); Leroutier (2022); Burke and Kurniawati (2018); Burke et al. (2017); Ruhnau et al. (2023); UBA (2024).

slides.title: About 1–2% per $10 a tonne in transport and heating; several times more in power
slides.caption: Measured cuts against the carbon price or equivalent (log scale); gray curves mark 1% and 10% per $10 a tonne.

points.text: Germany 1.4–2.0% per $10, Switzerland 0.7–1.6%, Sweden about 0.8%, US 1.0–1.3% in one year.
German gas and Indonesian fuel under 2% per $10.

slides.source: Author's calculation; working paper 5.5, Figure 1 and Table 12.

slides.title: Transport and heating respond slowly, because cars and boilers last

points.text: fuel use per person fell only after three to four years, then 10–15% by 2005.
transport CO₂ −5% in the short run and −19% in the long run.
no measurable response at CHF 12–36 a tonne; house owners cut heating fuel 12–14% at CHF 60–84.
German household gas +130% cut use by a fifth to a quarter within months; people turn the heating down before they replace the boiler.

slides.source: Runst and Höhle (2022); Pretis (2022); Francescutto and Mathys (2022); Ruhnau et al. (2023).

slides.title: Britain's carbon price floor drove coal out of power, because gas plants stood ready

stats.label: coal's share of British electricity generation, 2012 to 2019
rise in coal plants' fuel cost from the carbon price in 2015, against +30% for gas
power-sector CO₂ a year over 2013–2017, against a synthetic Britain

slides.text: A total carbon price of $14–36 a tonne reversed the order in which coal and gas plants ran, then closed coal plants. Counting only switching at existing plants, the cut was 6% at about €18 a tonne.
slides.source: BEIS (2017); Abrell, Kosch and Rausch (2022); Leroutier (2022); Gugler, Haxhimusa and Liebensteiner (2023).

slides.title: Design mattered as much as the price

points.text: demand fell 2–3 times more than for equal market price rises (British Columbia 2.9×, Sweden and the US about 3×), though part is buying ahead of announced rises.
Sweden cut its energy tax on petrol as the carbon tax more than doubled in 2001–04, and the transport gap barely widened.
British Columbia cut transport emissions but not, measurably, the total.
Germany's 2022 gas cut of 23% became a 1.3% fall in national emissions as power stations burned more coal.

slides.source: Lawley and Thivierge (2018); Andersson (2019); Li, Linn and Muehlegger (2014); Coglianese et al. (2017); Pretis (2022); UBA (2024).

slides.title: The cases support CPAT's gasoline response; its home-heating response looks too high
slides.note: Back-cast each case: give a model the data from before the policy and the prices that followed, and compare its predicted cut with the measured one.
slides.source: CPAT defaults for developing countries (Brief 5.4); working paper 5.5, Table 12 and Section 7.
